title: "4.3 Marginal Effects"
---

- The interpretation of a **marginal effect** in multinomial logit is all but identical to the interpretation in binary logit/probit:

  *MEM: The difference in Pr(y = j \| **x**) for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other control variables at their means*

  *AME: On average, the difference in Pr(y = j \| **x**) for a change in x~k~ of δ*

  - Here, we predict Pr(*y* = *j*), not Pr(*y*=1) as in the binary case
    - And have *J* total Pr(*y* = *j*), and thus *J* total MEs
- Decisions about where to hold the control variables follow the same logic as before (at their mean for MEM; average over observed values for AME; etc.)
- Decisions about the size of *δ* to use are the same
  - An instantaneous rate of change / slope (first derivative)
  - A finite change, AKA a discrete change
    - Can be any amount, e.g. one unit, SD, etc.
    - I find discrete changes most useful

## Marginal effects at the mean (MEM)

- Formulas for MEMs and AMEs are identical to before in linear and binary models. Only the formula for $\eta$ has changed (we use the formulas [above](4-2-predicted-probabilities.qmd#predicted-probabilities-in-multinomial-logit))
- For the MEM, we hold the control variables ($\mathbf{x}_{-k}$) at their means ($\overline{\mathbf{x}}$)

$$MEM = \eta(x_{k} = end, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}}) - \eta(x_{k} = start, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}})$$

- E.g., For a binary variable (e.g. *woman*):

$${MEM}_{binary} = \eta(x_{k} = 1, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}}) - \eta(x_{k} = 0, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}})$$

- E.g., For a continuous variable (e.g., *age*) could compare predictions at the mean and at the mean + SD:

$${MEM}_{continuous} = \eta(x_{k} = \overline{x}_{k} + SD, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}}) - \eta(x_{k} = \overline{x}_{k}, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \overline{\mathbf{x}})$$

- Because control variables were held at the sample means, can interpret MEM as effect *"for the average person"* in the data or someone *"average on all other variables included in the model"*

## Average marginal effects (AMEs)

- For an AME, we first compute a marginal effect for each observation in the data with the control variables held at their observed values for that specific observation ($\mathbf{x}_{-k,i}$):

$${ME}_{i} = \eta(x_{k} = {end}_{i}, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k,i}) - \eta(x_{k} = {start}_{i}, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k,i})$$

- The **average marginal effect** (AME) averages these effects over all observations in the data:

$$AME = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i = 1}^{N}\left\{\eta(x_{k} = {end}_{i}, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k,i}) - \eta(x_{k} = {start}_{i}, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k,i})\right\}$$

- Thus, the AME is interpreted as the effect "on average" in the data

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(nnet)            # multinomial logit: multinom()
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tdmize/Rfunctions/main/ME_helper_functions.R")

# Center changes in continuous IVs on each observation's value
options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center")

gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

gss <- gss |> filter(year >= 2016 & year <= 2021)

# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
gss <- gss[c("polviews3", "age", "woman", "race3", "college", "married", "parent",
  "faminc", "employed", "conserv")]
gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss[c("conserv", "age", "woman", "race3", "college",
  "married", "parent", "faminc")]), ]

# Treat binary/nominal variables as factors
gss <- gss |>
  mutate(across(c(polviews3, woman, race3, college, married, parent, employed), as_factor)) |>
  droplevels()

# 3 category political views var
pol3mod <- multinom(polviews3 ~ age + woman + race3 + college + married + parent +
  faminc + employed, data = gss, trace = FALSE)

# AMEs +SD of age
avg_comparisons(pol3mod, variables = list(age = sd(gss$age)))
```

> *On average, a standard deviation increase in age (about 17 years) is associated with a 0.049 higher probability of identifying as conservative. A standard deviation increase in age, in contrast, leads to a 0.029 lower probability of identifying as moderate and a 0.020 lower probability of identifying as liberal*

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
[Interpretation tip:]{.underline} A separate sentence for each ME can be tedious. I often use the strategy of grouping effects in the same direction into one sentence. At most, you would then need three sentences: one for positive effects, one for null effects, and one for negative effects.
:::

## Plots of binary/nominal IVs

- For binary/nominal IVs, you only sometimes need a plot. It depends on how complicated the patterns are and how many categories you have of your IV and your DV
- All else equal, the more categories of the IV and/or the DV makes it more likely you will need a plot
  - Often helpful to make the plot to guide your interpretations even if the plot does not make it into the final article
- One option for binary/nominal IVs is to plot each set of predictions
  - **Pro**: These are intuitive to understand
  - **Con**: These do not explicitly show the test of an effect of the focal IV

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

- In R, use [**plot_predictions**](https://marginaleffects.com/bonus/plot.html), the **facet_wrap** function, and include **"group"** in the **by** function for a fairly nice dot plot
  - Make sure to specify the counterfactual **grid_type** in **newdata** for average predictions, rather than predictions for modal person


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 4.3.a - Show pr() of each group; dot plot
plot_predictions(pol3mod, by = c("college", "group"),
  newdata = datagrid(college = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, .1), limits = c(0, .5)) +
  labs(title = "[4.3.a] Probability of Each Political View Based on Educational Degree",
    x = NULL, y = "Pr(Political View)") +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot", legend.position = "none")
```

## Plots of marginal effects for binary IVs

- An alternative to plotting the predictions for each category of a binary/nominal IV is to plot the marginal effect for that variable (e.g., *college*: 1 vs 0)
  - Note this is the difference between each set of two bars above
    - **Pro**: Half as many bars to plot; has information on significance test of the effect
    - **Con**: Less intuitive to readers---needs more explanation
- Make sure to always include a **subtitle( )** or a **note( )** on these plots to help readers interpret the direction of the effects

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### ME inequality for nominal IVs

- Combining nominal or ordinal IVs with nominal or ordinal outcomes presents a challenge of an overwhelming number of predictions and marginal effects to examine
  - The \# of MEs for nominal/ordinal IVs in nominal/ordinal DV models = the \# of outcome categories \* the \# of pairwise comparisons of the nominal/ordinal IV
    - For a nominal independent variable with *L* categories and a nominal or ordinal outcome with $\Lambda$ outcome categories

$$\#\ of\ MEs = \Lambda * \frac{L(L - 1)}{2}$$

- One solution, simplify down to the ME inequality per outcome category $\lambda$ ([Mize and Han 2025](/research/mize_han_socsci_2025.qmd))

$${ME\ inequality}_{\lambda} \equiv |average\ weighted\ ME\ inequality|_{\lambda} = \sum_{a = 1}^{L}\sum_{b = 2;\ b > a}^{L}\frac{w_{a,b}}{L - 1} \left|\eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = a, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*}) - \eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = b, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*})\right|$$

*"This procedure will greatly simplify interpretation. For example, with a four-category DV and a six-category IV there are*

$$\Lambda * \frac{L(L - 1)}{2} = 4 * \frac{6(6 - 1)}{2} = 4 * 15 = 60$$

*60 marginal effects. In contrast, there are always only* $\Lambda$ ${ME\ inequality}_{\lambda}$ *measures; in this case, four."* ([Mize and Han 2025](/research/mize_han_socsci_2025.qmd))

- In Stata, use the [**meinequality**](/software/meinequality/index.qmd) command or the **meinequality** option of **mecompare**
  - In R, use the [**meineq()** function on **avg_comparisons**](/software/meinequality_r/index.qmd)

## Total marginal effects

- With a linear or binary outcome, a single ME summarizes the total effect of a continuous or binary IV
  - [Mize and Han (2025)](/research/mize_han_socsci_2025.qmd) suggest that similar logic can be applied in nominal and ordinal outcome models by aggregating the effect of a single IV across each outcome category
  - That is, an IV's total effect is its holistic effect across all outcomes
    - Then, the **total ME** statistic is simply the sum of all the marginal effects for that IV (using absolute values) divided by two\*

$$total\ ME = \frac{\sum_{\lambda = 1}^{\Lambda}\left|\eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = end, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*}) - \eta_{\lambda}(x_{k} = start, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}_{-k}^{*})\right|}{2}$$

> *"The total ME represents the proportion of observations that are predicted to change outcomes given a change in the independent variable. Put another way, this represents the complete effect of the independent variable across all outcome categories."* ([Mize and Han 2025](/research/mize_han_socsci_2025.qmd))

\*The *total ME* is divided by two to account for the fact that MEs in multi-outcome models are symmetric/zero-sum.

- In Stata, use the [**totalme**](/software/totalme/index.qmd) command or the **totalme** option of **mecompare**
  - In R, use the [**totalme()** function on **avg_comparisons**](/software/totalme_r/index.qmd)

### Total marginal effect inequality statistics

- We can combine the *ME inequality* approach to summarizing nominal and ordinal IV effects with the *total ME* approach developed in the prior section to obtain a single summary measure
  - In this case, the *total ME inequality* for a nominal or ordinal IV is simply the sum of the ${ME\ inequality}_{\lambda}$ measures divided by two.

$$total\ ME\ inequality = \frac{\sum_{\lambda = 1}^{\Lambda}{ME\ inequality}_{\lambda}}{2}$$

- The default statistic for **totalme** after a nominal model is the total ME inequality

### Total marginal effects for comparing effects

- Total marginal effects are especially helpful if you want to compare effects
  - How would you determine if age or college had a larger effect when there are four MEs for each IV?
    - The total ME provides one \# per IV
- Tests of interaction and cross-model comparisons like mediation similarly benefit from a total ME
  - Is the effect of age different for men and women?
    - Instead of testing per outcome category, total ME gives one answer
  - Does SES explain part of the racial-ethnic gaps?
    - Calculate a total ME for *race* in a model with and without SES
